newsitem.title: USA: G7 summit takes compromise stand on global warming.
newsitem.headline: G7 summit takes compromise stand on global warming.

text.p: Under heavy U.S. pressure, the Group of Seven industrialised nations summit in Denver took a compromise stand on global warming on Sunday that European Commission President Jacques Santer called disappointing.

The annual summit, which wound up the day before the United Nations opens a week-long environmental "Earth Summit" in New York, issued a communique that fell short of EU calls for a clear target for cuts in gases that cause the "greenhouse effect."

It said the G7 states wanted clear and realistic targets for carbon emission cuts but avoided the target -- a 15 percent reduction by the year 2010 -- that the EU has agreed as its position for the Earth Summit.

Delegation officials said Clinton, apparently concerned about unpopular energy price hikes that any tough agreement could bring, warned his partners the G7 members should not make problems for each other.
Santer said: "I am frankly disappointed that not all our partners were able here and now to take quantified commitments on the reduction of greenhouse gas emissions."
"We must stop the degradation of our climate. The future of the planet is at stake," he said.

The environment dispute produced one of the few points of discord at the Denver summit of the G7, the forum of leading industrialised states that meets annually to set broad economic and political policy lines for the next year.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl said the issue split the summit into two blocs, the EU members -- Britain, France, Germany and Italy -- against the U.S., Japan and Canada.

The U.S. accounts for almost a quarter of all greenhouse gases emitted around the world when fossil fuels like oil and coal are burned. Scientists say these emissions will lead to dangerous climate changes in the next century if unchecked.

The summit communique said the G7 states wanted a "strong agreement" with quantified and legally-binding emission targets by the time of a United Nations conference on climate change in Kyoto in December.
It spoke of "meaningful, realistic and equitable targets" and dropped stronger references in earlier drafts about significant or substantial reductions in emission levels.
Santer, who attends the G7 summits, said the EU was still committed to cutting greenhouse gases to 15 percent of their 1990 levels by 2010.
"We will continue to press our partners at the Kyoto Conference," he said.
Kohl, a driving force in the EU's push for a tougher line on climate change, echoed Santer's view.
"I think we'll succeed in finding a formula by Kyoto," Kohl told ZDF television. "We have a few months' time."
Clinton's opposition to reduction targets in the communique earned him open criticism from some summit participants.
French President Jacques Chirac said: "There is a real divergence of views between, on one hand the Europeans and on the other the Americans -- not Canada, the United States."
The special U.N. General Assembly session in New York next week will discuss progress in fighting global warming since the first Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro five years ago.
